newsitem.title: USA: U.S. congressman calls for MIR safety review.
newsitem.headline: U.S. congressman calls for MIR safety review.

text.p: The chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives Science Committee on Wednesday called on NASA to begin an immediate safety review of the Russian space station Mir before any more U.S. astronauts went on board for a long-term stay.

"I, for one, can no longer sit idly by as mishap after mishap occurs while we continue to plan the next shuttle mission to Mir hoping for, but not really expecting, the mission will succeed without a potentially life-threatening situation," Representative James Sensenbrenner, Republican of Wisconsin, said.
The Mir space station carrying U.S. astronaut Michael Foale and Russians Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin collided on Wednesday with a cargo craft during a manual docking exercise.
The crew was in no immediate danger but faced power problems, Russian space officials said.

"Our prayers are with the crew on board Mir. The highest priority is to ensure their safety," Sensenbrenner said at a news conference. He noted that NASA administrator Dan Goldin told him this morning the immediate danger had passed.

Sensenbrenner called for NASA to begin a comprehensive review of safety of Mir immediately and asked the space agency to comply voluntarily with legislation that would bar more U.S. astronauts from going on board Mir for a long-term stay until the safety tests are passed.

The House recently passed a bill, the Civilian Space Authorisation, which contained a requirement that no U.S. astronaut be placed on board Mir for a long-term stay until the National Aeronatics and Space Administration certifies to Congress that the space station meets or exceeds U.S. safety standards. It is not yet law.

Sensenbrenner asked Goldin to reply within the next week on whether he will comply with the legislation. "The review should be initiated immediately and be concluded in advance of any decision to send the STS-86 crew to Mir as scheduled for September," he said. While Goldin had noted an outside review had been completed, Sensenbrenner said this review was not an acceptable substitute for the one called for in the legislation.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said President Bill Clinton remained "committed to the programme."
He said Clinton had been briefed by his science and technology adviser, Jack Gibbons, about the Mir accident.
"NASA right now is in very close consultation with its Russia counterpart. They're exploring all aspects of the problem and trouble-shooting various aspects of the problem," McCurry said.
